scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Sigalegale puppet dance originates from the Batak Toba people of Samosir Island, Northern Sumatra, Indonesia.
It is linked to a local legend about Nai Manggale, a childless woman who instructed her husband to create a lifesize puppet of herself to prevent her spirit from cursing him after death.
Early 20th-century missionary Johannes Warneck described the use of the puppet in funerary ceremonies for wealthy men who died without heirs.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The Sigalegale dance is performed during papurpur sapata funerary ceremonies for persons of high rank who died without offspring.
It serves to dispel the curse of dying childless and to placate the spirit of the deceased.
The puppet acts as a symbolic child to perform funerary rites, ensuring the deceased's spirit is honored and does no harm to the community.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The Sigalegale puppet is dressed in traditional Batak costume, including a shawl, headdress, and gold jewelry.
The puppet is life-sized and mounted on a large wheeled platform.
The setting is a funerary ceremony on Samosir Island, often held outdoors in the village, including a procession to the market where meat is distributed.
